'''Ueli Schibler''' (born June 16, 1947)<ref name="foundation louis jeantet">{{cite web|title=Professeur Ueli Schibler, EMBO/EMBL Conference|url=http://www.embl.it/aboutus/science_society/conferences/conference_2004/participants/schibler/}}</ref> is a Swiss biologist, chronobiologist and a professor at the [[University of Geneva]]. His research has contributed significantly to the field of chronobiology and the understanding of circadian clocks in the body. Several of his studies have demonstrated strong evidence for the existence of robust, self-sustaining circadian clocks in the peripheral tissues.<ref name="Reppert & Weaver" />

Schibler has studied the molecular biology of gene [[Gene expression|expression]]s and chronobiology since his serendipitous discovery of a protein expressed in a strong circadian fashion. He is also a current editor for several academic journals, such as [[PLoS Biology]], [[European Molecular Biology Organization|EMBOReports]] and [http://webarchive.loc.gov/all/20110604002300/http://jbr.sagepub.com/ Journal of Biological Rhythms].

==Biography==
===Early life and family===
Ueli Schibler was born in 1947 in [[Olten]], a small town in Switzerland. His father was a sculptor who manufactured [[monument]]s, and his mother helped manage the family business. In 1972, Ueli Schibler married with Monika Schibler, who he met at the age of 19, and had a son and daughter. His son was born in [[Philadelphia]] in 1977 when Ueli was a postdoc at [[Fox Chase Cancer Center]] while his daughter was born in 1979, one year after they moved back to Switzerland. Currently, Ueli Schibler resides in Switzerland and works in [[University of Geneva]] as a professor at the Department of [[Molecular Biology]]. Monika and Ueli Schibler are now grandparents and have three grandchildren.

===Education and academic experiences===

Over 5 years from 1967 to 1972, Schibler pursued the study of [[biology]], [[biochemistry]], and [[chemistry]] at the [[University of Bern]], approximately seventy kilometers from his hometown of [[Olten]]. At graduation, he was awarded a Diploma in Biology. Afterwards, he continued his education there, eventually receiving his PhD diploma with [[Latin Honors]] in 1975 for his work on [[ribosomal RNA]] in the context of [[vertebrate]] [[evolution]].<ref name="foundation louis jeantet" /> He then obtained a postdoctoral fellowship from the Swiss National Science Foundation and worked at the laboratory of Robert Perry, who was based at the [[Fox Chase Cancer Center]] in [[Philadelphia]] for two years. In 1978, he became a junior group leader at [[ISREC|The Swiss Institute for Experimental Cancer Research]]. In 1981, he was promoted to the status of a group leader with tenure, where he remained for three years. Finally, in 1984, he obtained a full professorship at the Department of Molecular Biology at the [[University of Geneva]], where he currently resides.<ref name="F1000 Prime">{{cite web|title=Professeur Ueli Schibler, F1000 Prime Profile|url=http://f1000.com/prime/thefaculty/member/2010765042386619|access-date=2015-04-06|archive-date=2015-05-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150505192950/http://f1000.com/prime/thefaculty/member/2010765042386619|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Serendipitous discovery===
Schibler was thrust into the world of [[chronobiology]] on a single chance discovery. While examining [[Transcription (genetics)|transcription]] of serum [[albumin]] gene in the liver, they discovered a DNA Binding Protein ([[DBP (gene)|DBP]]) for the albumin [[Promoter (genetics)|promoter]] that happened to be rhythmic in its expression. While they initially thought that the underlying mechanism was the rhythmic secretion of [[hormones]], it became clear that the rhythmic expression of DBP was driven instead by cell-autonomous [[oscillators]] that are entrained by the master clock in the [[Suprachiasmatic Nucleus]] (SCN). Schibler and his colleagues followed this line of inquiry into the field of chronobiology.
<ref name="Foundation2004">{{cite book|author1=Preitner N|author2=Brown S|author3= Ripperger J|author4=Le-Minh N|author5=Damiola F|author6=Schibler U |others=Novartis Foundation|title=Molecular Clocks and Light Signalling|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ANS8-Ang9CwC&pg=PA89|date=25 June 2004|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-0-470-09082-4|page=89}}</ref>

===Current research===
A timing system with circadian clocks is closely related to all behaviors in mammals. Schibler is currently doing researches on how biological clock works. Schibler together with his research team in University of Geneva have developed a technique called "Synthetic Tandem Repeat PROMoter (STAR-PROM) screening" which can assist identify [[transcription factors]] and their functions in peripheral cells so that to figure out how circadian gene expression is governed rhythmically with regulatory mechanisms in [[cultured cells]].<ref name="PHYS.ORG">{{cite web|title=Identifying all factors modulating gene expression is actually possible, PHYS.ORG|url=http://phys.org/news/2013-01-factors-modulating-gene.html|access-date=2015-04-23|archive-date=2015-11-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151106053317/http://phys.org/news/2013-01-factors-modulating-gene.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Scientific achievements==

===Evidence of circadian clocks in peripheral tissues===
While at the Department of Molecular Biology at the University of Geneva, Schibler's research team unexpectedly came across [[DBP (gene)|DBP]], a [[Transcriptional regulation|transcriptional regulatory protein]] whose expression was found to be robustly [[Circadian rhythm|circadian]] in the liver. This discovery prompted Schibler and his team to further investigate the role of [[circadian clock]]s in peripheral tissue.<ref name="foundation louis jeantet" />

In a 1998 study, Schibler and his team published a paper providing strong evidence for the existence of circadian clocks in mammalian peripheral tissue.<ref name="Reppert & Weaver">{{cite journal|last1=Reppert|first1=Steven|last2=Weaver|first2=David|title=Coordination of Circadian Timing in Mammals|journal=Nature|date=29 August 2002|volume=418|issue=6901|pages=935–941|doi=10.1038/nature00965|pmid=12198538|bibcode=2002Natur.418..935R}}</ref> The study demonstrated that "immortalized rat [[fibroblast]]s", frozen in cell culture for 25 years, were still capable of expressing strong circadian rhythms. After an initial serum-shock, both rat-1 fibroblasts and H35 hepatoma cells demonstrated cyclic [[Messenger RNA|mRNA]] expression of clock genes [[PER1|rper1]] and [[PER2|rper2]], and [[Rev-ErbA alpha|Rev-Erbα]], and the clock controlled genes [[TEF (gene)|Tef]] and [[DBP (gene)|Dbp]], with a period of nearly 24 hours and a phase relationship closely mimicking those observed in rat liver cells [[in vivo]].<ref name="Balsalobre et al.">{{cite journal|last1=Balsalobre|first1=Aurélio|last2=Damiola|first2=Francesca|last3=Schibler|first3=Ueli|title=A Serum Shock Induces Circadian Gene Expression In Mammalian Tissue Culture Cells|journal=Cell|date=12 June 1998|volume=93|issue=6|pages=929–937|pmid=9635423|doi=10.1016/s0092-8674(00)81199-x|doi-access=free}}</ref>

====Circadian rhythms in peripheral tissue persist during cell division====
In a 2004 study that provided further evidence for the existence of self-sustained, autonomous oscillators in the peripheral tissue,<ref name="Takahashi et al.">{{cite journal|last1=Takahashi|first1=Joseph|last2=Hong|first2=Hee-Kyung|last3=Ko|first3=Caroline|last4=McDearmon|first4=Erin|title=The genetics of mammalian circadian order and disorder: implications for physiology and disease|journal=Nature Reviews Genetics|date=9 October 2008|volume=9|issue=10|pages=764–775|doi=10.1038/nrg2430|pmid=18802415|pmc=3758473}}</ref> Schibler and his colleagues found evidence for interaction between the circadian clock and the timing of cell division. Single-cell recordings revealed how circadian gene expression in fibroblasts persists during [[cell division]], and how cell division can phase shift the circadian cycle of the dividing cells.<ref name="Nagoshi et al.">{{cite journal|last1=Nagoshi|first1=Emi|last2=Saini|first2=Camille|last3=Bauer|first3=Christoph|last4=Laroche|first4=Thierry|last5=Naef|first5=Felix|last6=Schibler|first6=Ueli|title=Circadian Gene Expression in Individual Fibroblasts: Cell-Autonomous and Self-Sustained Oscillators Pass Time to Daughter Cells|journal=Cell|date=24 November 2004|volume=119|issue=5|pages=693–705|doi=10.1016/j.cell.2004.11.015|pmid=15550250|doi-access=free}}</ref> Due to the central role of Period [[Period (gene)|(PER)]] and Cryptochrome [[Cryptochrome|(CRY)]] proteins in the [[negative feedback loop]] of the circadian clock, Schibler and colleagues posited the PER-CRY complex concentration to be the likely determinant of the phase of the clock.<ref name="Bae et al.">{{cite journal|last1=Bae|first1=Kiho|last2=Jin|first2=Xiaowei|last3=Maywood|first3=Elizabeth|last4=Hastings|first4=Michael|last5=Reppert|first5=Steven|last6=Weaver|first6=David|title=Differential Functions of mPer1, mPer2, and mPer3 in the SCN Circadian Clock|journal=Neuron|date=May 2001|volume=30|issue=2|pages=525–536|doi=10.1016/S0896-6273(01)00302-6|pmid=11395012|doi-access=free}}</ref> When cell division frequency was plotted against circadian time, this yielded a highly nonrandom distribution, suggesting a gating mechanism of mitosis by the circadian clock<ref name="Nagoshi et al."/>

===Feeding Rhythms are Strong Zeitgebers for Peripheral Clocks===

Schibler and his colleagues have also studied mechanisms by which peripheral oscillators are synchronized within the body. In 2000, they conducted experiments on the effects of restricted feeding time on mice and observed that the phase of peripheral oscillators – but not that of the [[suprachiasmatic nucleus|SCN]] – gradually adapted to imposed feeding-fasting rhythms within a week or two.<ref name="Damiola et al.">{{cite journal|last1=Damiola|first1=Francesca|last2=Le Minh|first2=Nguyet|last3=Preitner|first3=Nicolas|last4=Kornmann|first4=Benoît|last5=Fleury-Olela|first5=Fabienne|last6=Ueli|first6=Schibler|title=Restricted feeding uncouples circadian oscillators in peripheral tissues from the central pacemaker in the suprachiasmatic nucleus|journal=Genes & Development|date=9 October 2000|doi=10.1101/gad.183500|pmid=11114885|volume=14|issue=23|pmc=317100|pages=2950–61}}</ref> These results showed that feeding time functions as a potent Zeitgeber for peripheral cells, but not for the SCN. Schibler and colleagues posited that the SCN can synchronize peripheral clocks simply by imposing rest-activity cycles, which in turn drive feeding-fasting cycles. However, in the meantime they discovered additional pathways involved in the phase-resetting of peripheral clocks, such as signaling by [[Glucocorticoid|glucocorticoid hormones]],<ref name="Balsalobre et al">{{cite journal|last1=Balsalobre|first1=Aurélio|last2=Brown|first2=Steven|last3=Marcacci|first3=Lysiane|last4=Tronche|first4=Francois|last5=Kellendonk|first5=Christoph|last6=Reichardt|first6=Holger|last7=Schütz|first7=Günther|last8=Schibler|first8=Ueli|title=Resetting of Circadian Time in Peripheral Tissues by Glucocorticoid Signaling|journal=Science|date=September 2000|volume=289|issue=29|pages=2344–2347|doi=10.1126/science.289.5488.2344|pmid=11009419}}</ref> body temperature,<ref name="Brown et al.">{{cite journal|last1=Brown|first1=Steven|last2=Zumbrunn|first2=Gottlieb|last3=Fleury-Olela|first3=Fabienne|last4=Preitner|first4=Nicolas|last5=Schibler|first5=Ueli|title=Rhythms of Mammalian Body Temperature Can Sustain Peripheral Circadian Clocks|journal=Cell|date=17 September 2002|volume=12|issue=18|pages=1574–1583|doi=10.1016/S0960-9822(02)01145-4|pmid=12372249|doi-access=free}}</ref> and [[actin]] dynamics.<ref name="Gerber et al.">{{cite journal|last1=Gerber|first1=Alan|last2=Esnault|first2=Cyril|last3=Aubert|first3=Gregory|last4=Treisman|first4=Richard|last5=Pralong|first5=Francois|last6=Schibler|first6=Ueli|title=Blood-Borne Circadian Signal Stimulates Daily Oscillations in Actin Dynamics and SRF Activity|journal=Cell|date=31 January 2013|volume=152|issue=3|pages=492–503|doi=10.1016/j.cell.2012.12.027|pmid=23374345|doi-access=free|hdl=1871.1/75055017-e93c-409f-b191-c136ffc443cd|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

===REV-ERBα is a Major Regulator of the Circadian Clock===

In 2002, Schibler and his colleagues identified the nuclear orphan receptor [[Rev-ErbA alpha|REV-ERBα]] as the major regulator of expression of the circadian gene [[ARNTL|Bmal1]] in both the SCN and peripheral tissues. BMAL-1, as a [[heterodimer]] with [[Clock (gene)|CLOCK]] activates the transcription of the components of the negative limb encoding [[Period (gene)|PER]] and [[Cryptochrome|CRY]] repressor proteins. Together, the feedback loop of the positive limb and its effects on the negative limb produce the mammalian circadian rhythms in clock gene expression. REV-ERBα and its paralog [[Rev-ErbA beta|REV-ERBβ]] are the molecular links between these two feedback loops.<ref name="Cho et al.">{{cite journal|last1=Cho|first1=Han|last2=Zhao|first2=Xuan|last3=Hatori|first3=Megumi|last4=Yu|first4=Ruth|last5=Barish|first5=Grant|last6=Lam|first6=Michael|last7=Chong|first7=Ling-Wa|last8=DiTacchio|first8=Luciano|last9=Atkins|first9=Annette|last10=Glass|first10=Christopher|last11=Liddle|first11=Christopher|last12=Auwrex|first12=Johan|last13=Downes|first13=Michael|last14=Panda|first14=Satchidananda|last15=Evans|first15=Ronald|title=Regulation of Circadian Behavior and Metabolism by Rev-erbα and Rev-erbβ|journal=Nature|date=29 March 2012|pages=123–127|doi=10.1038/nature11048|pmid=22460952|volume=485|issue=7396|pmc=3367514}}</ref><ref name="Bugge et al.">{{cite journal|last1=Bugge|first1=Anne|last2=Feng|first2=Dan|last3=Everett|first3=Logan|last4=Briggs|first4=Erika|last5=Mullican|first5=Shannon|last6=Wang|first6=Fenfen|last7=Jager|first7=Jennifer|last8=Lazer|first8=Mitchell|title=Rev-erbα and Rev-erbβ coordinately protect the circadian clock and normal metabolic function|journal=Genes & Development|date=1 April 2012|pages=657–667|doi=10.1101/gad.186858.112|pmid=22474260|volume=26|issue=7|pmc=3323877}}</ref>
